subject: Critical Thinking
title: Validity vs. Soundness: The Critical Distinction
description: A micro-lesson that makes Validity vs. Soundness: The Critical Distinction usable.

hook.text: 'All fish can fly. A salmon is a fish. Therefore, salmon can fly.' This argument is logically valid.

buildup.text: Valid means the conclusion follows from the premises. It says nothing about whether the premises are true.

discovery.text: Sound means valid AND the premises are actually true. Soundness is what we really want.

twist.text: Many persuasive arguments are valid but unsound — the logic works but it's built on false premises.

climax.text: Checking validity is a logic skill. Checking soundness requires knowledge of the world.

punchline.text: Good logic with bad facts still gives you bad answers.

quiz.question: What makes an argument sound rather than merely valid?
options: It's valid AND has true premises

details.summary: Validity means an argument's conclusion necessarily follows from its premises; soundness means the argument is both valid and has true premises. Many persuasive arguments are valid but unsound because they rest on false assumptions.
details.whyItMatters: Distinguishing validity from soundness prevents you from accepting logically structured arguments built on false foundations.
takeaways: Valid arguments have correct logical form
Sound arguments are valid with true premises
An argument can be valid yet completely wrong

faq.question: Can you give an example of a valid but unsound argument?
faq.answer: All fish can fly. Salmon are fish. Therefore, salmon can fly. The logic is perfect, but the first premise is false, so the argument is valid but unsound.

faq.question: Why is the validity-soundness distinction practically important?
faq.answer: It shows that logical structure alone is not enough. You must also verify premises. Propaganda often uses valid-looking arguments with cleverly disguised false premises.
